case_study_insert.main_stem: Tanner & Rowe Boutique (TNR) is a private limited company in the online fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2013 by Imogen Tanner in Manchester, the business sells women's clothing through its own website and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. TNR plans to invest $620,000 in a new e-commerce fulfilment warehouse and click-and-collect hub, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $26.00, and sells 30,000 units a year. TNR faces two operational problems: the online return rate has risen to 8.5% and customers have complained about sizing errors.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: E-commerce Operations Log — Q4 2026: The online store fulfilled 7,200 orders last month at an average delivery time of 4.1 days. The product return rate rose to 8.5% from 5.2%, and complaints about garment sizing reached 64 while the fulfilment error rate was 2.3%. A survey of 450 online shoppers found 71% want free returns and 58% check delivery speed before ordering. A training needs analysis shows 12 of the 38 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new returns system; off-the-job training at the local college costs $700 per employee. Reworking a returned garment costs $9 per unit.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Tanner & Rowe Boutique as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2027): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing debt-servicing costs for firms with variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% from $13.41 to $14.10 an hour from April 2027, lifting wage bills across retail and fulfilment. (3) Parcel-delivery and packaging input costs have increased 9.3% year-on-year, while consumer spending on online fashion fell 2.1% over the same period.

questions.question_text: TNR plans to fund part of its $620,000 e-commerce fulfilment warehouse with a $400,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TNR of using $220,000 retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $220,000 of retained profit avoids interest payments and capital repayments on that portion of the $620,000 warehouse, protecting TNR's cash flow while it already services a $400,000 ten-year bank loan. With fixed costs of $180,000 a year and an 8.5% return rate that creates reworking costs, every dollar saved in interest can be spent on reducing sizing errors rather than paid to lenders, and the $26.00 selling price does not have to be raised to cover finance charges.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk, so the new click-and-collect hub is not endangered if online demand falls short of the 30,000-unit target. It also preserves Imogen Tanner's control of the private limited company: no lender can impose conditions on how the fulfilment operation is run, allowing the democratic leadership team to redirect spending quickly towards the 71% of shoppers who want free returns. Retaining the $220,000 also signals financial strength to suppliers when TNR negotiates delivery terms amid 9.3% parcel-cost inflation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to TNR's funding decision, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: TNR is promoting the launch of its click-and-collect hub. Consider local radio advertising, social media advertising, or a fashion influencer partnership. Which should TNR choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio advertising: Radio is cheap and can reach Manchester shoppers near the new click-and-collect hub, with quick turnaround for a launch message. However, TNR sells through its own website to a national audience, so a local audience is too narrow to drive the 30,000 units a year needed, and radio cannot show the garments that generate the 8.5% sizing-related returns.

Social media advertising: Paid social campaigns can target lookalike audiences of online fashion shoppers, show products visually to cut sizing confusion, and direct buyers straight to the website or click-and-collect hub. Results are measurable and scalable within the $620,000 expansion budget, but costs per click can rise sharply with fashion competition, and ads may be ignored without credible content.

Fashion influencer partnership: Influencers demonstrate fit and styling on real bodies, directly tackling the sizing complaints behind the 8.5% return rate, and their credibility appeals to the 58% of surveyed shoppers who check delivery speed and the 71% who want free returns. Reach can be national without the wastage of radio, though fees are less predictable and depend on the influencer's reputation.

Recommendation: TNR should choose social media advertising, with a small influencer test layered on top. Social advertising gives the widest measurable national reach at controllable cost and can carry the free-returns message that 71% of shoppers want; influencers alone are less predictable and slower to scale, while local radio is rejected as too narrow for a web-based business aiming at 30,000 units. Radio can be used later only for the Manchester click-and-collect catchment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TNR with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of TNR with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and influencers lose.

questions.question_text: TNR's return rate has reached 8.5% and sizing complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for TNR of using democratic leadership within its flat organisational structure.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the workforce of 38 a real voice in how the returns process is organised, so packers and customer-service staff can suggest clearer size guides and better folding notes. Because the flat organisational structure has few layers, those suggestions reach Imogen Tanner immediately and can be tested at once, directly attacking the 8.5% return rate and the 64 sizing complaints recorded in the operations log.

Point 2: Involvement raises ownership and motivation, which matters when 12 staff still lack on-the-job training on the new returns system. Staff who help design the returns flow are more likely to follow it accurately, cutting the 2.3% fulfilment error rate and the $9 cost of reworking each returned garment. In a business with fixed costs of $180,000 a year, fewer returns protect the $26.00 selling price and the contribution needed to justify the $620,000 warehouse investment, while democratic decisions make it easier to introduce the free-returns policy wanted by 71% of shoppers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TNR's return rate, complaints and flat structure.

questions.question_text: TNR must train 12 staff on the new returns system. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should TNR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the returns bench is specific to TNR's own system and quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps the 12 staff handling orders while they learn, protecting the 7,200 orders fulfilled each month and progress on the 8.5% return rate. Its weaknesses are that trainers are working staff whose own tasks suffer, bad habits may be copied, and there is no external certificate for auditors.

Off-the-job training: The local college course costs $700 per employee, so training all 12 staff would cost $8,400 — small beside the $620,000 warehouse investment. It gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification that may help when TNR negotiates with national retail partners. Against this, the 12 staff are away from the fulfilment line, which could lengthen the current 4.1-day delivery time and annoy the 58% of shoppers who check delivery speed; the generic content may also miss TNR's exact returns software.

Decision: TNR should choose on-the-job training first, followed by short college sessions for the most senior operators. On-the-job training is cheaper, immediately relevant and avoids losing capacity while the return rate is 8.5% and orders run at 7,200 a month. Full off-the-job training is rejected because $8,400 of fees and 12 absent staff would disrupt the $620,000 hub's launch; college modules can be added once the system stabilises and the $9 reworking cost per return has fallen. Because 12 of the 38 staff are affected, sending them all to college at once would disrupt the 7,200 monthly orders; a phased rota keeps the click-and-collect hub running while the skills are built.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TNR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of TNR.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of TNR with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TNR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($26.00 − $14.00) = $180,000 ÷ $12.00 = 15,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 15,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $26.00 − $14.00 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TNR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing break-even output of 15,000 units with actual sales of 30,000 units gives a margin of safety of 15,000 units, showing how far demand can fall before the $620,000 warehouse becomes a loss-making commitment.
2. Contribution per unit of $12.00 lets managers model discounts: a $2.00 price cut would leave $10.00 contribution, so they can judge whether the extra volume needed to keep covering $180,000 fixed costs is realistic.
3. Knowing the 15,000-unit break-even point helps test whether the $400,000 bank loan can be serviced from profits before the click-and-collect hub expands further.
4. Unit cost of $20.00 ($180,000 ÷ 30,000 units = $6.00 plus the $14.00 variable cost) can be tracked each quarter to show whether the 8.5% return rate and $9 reworking cost are pushing costs up.

questions.model_answer: (i) break-even output = 15,000 units | (ii) contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 15,000 units against 30,000-unit sales; discount modelling on $12.00 contribution; servicing the $400,000 bank loan; unit cost of $20.00 to attack the 8.5% return rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TNR's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TNR's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.10 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 + $65,000 + $25,000 = $180,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $80,000 + $30,000 = $180,000. Dividing these by current liabilities of $120,000 in 2024 and $100,000 in 2025 gives the two labelled figures. Removing stock leaves $90,000 in 2024 and $110,000 in 2025, so the second pair of figures follows from the same current liabilities.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. The first ratio rose from 1.50 to 1.80 because current liabilities fell from $120,000 to $100,000 while current assets held at $180,000, giving a wider cushion for the $620,000 warehouse commitments. More importantly, the second measure improved from 0.75 to 1.10: TNR is no longer dependent on selling its $70,000 of inventories to meet short-term debts, which is valuable when an 8.5% return rate can leave stock unsellable. However, trade receivables climbed from $65,000 to $80,000, tying up cash that could fund the $9-per-unit reworking costs, and a $400,000 bank loan still requires regular interest payments if rates keep rising.

Conclusion: TNR's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the improvement is not reliant on inventory, so short-term solvency is genuinely better. The residual risk is slower-paying customers, so management should tighten credit control on the rising receivables before drawing further on the loan. Management should also watch the $30,000 cash balance, because one late payment from a major retail customer could quickly absorb the improvement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether TNR's position improved.

questions.question_text: TNR is considering introducing free returns on all online fashion orders. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TNR of this policy.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Free returns directly match the 71% of surveyed shoppers who want them and could reduce the deterrent that accompanies an 8.5% return rate, encouraging more orders at the $26.00 selling price. It strengthens TNR's competitive position against the 2.1% fall in online fashion spending and supports the 30,000-unit target that justifies the $620,000 fulfilment hub and its click-and-collect service.

Disadvantage: Each returned garment currently costs $9 to rework, so removing delivery charges shifts more of that cost onto TNR and cuts the $12.00 contribution earned on each sale. With fixed costs of $180,000 a year and variable costs of $14.00 a unit, a further rise in returns above the existing 8.5% would quickly absorb the margin, and the 5.2% historical return rate shows how quickly the position can change. TNR would need to monitor whether extra orders really cover the added reworking bill before extending the policy across the whole range.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TNR's research, costs and return rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.3% rise in parcel-delivery and packaging costs will affect TNR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If TNR's $400,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $180,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed-rate the immediate effect is zero. Higher rates may also deter the 71% of shoppers who want free returns from spending, but TNR can cap this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage rise (5.2%, to $14.10 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 38 but no hours worked or individual pay, so no honest annual wage total can be invented. Qualitatively the rise feeds straight into the cost of running the new fulfilment hub and cannot be avoided. It matters because labour supports 30,000 units and the $12.00 contribution; if productivity holds, the effect per unit is small, but if the 8.5% return rate keeps generating $9 reworking costs, unit labour costs will climb and squeeze the margin.

Parcel and packaging inflation (9.3%): Delivery is central to TNR's online model and 58% of shoppers check delivery speed, so cutting delivery quality to save money would lose sales. If the whole $14.00 variable cost rose by 9.3%, that would add 0.093 × $14.00 = $1.30 per unit, or 30,000 × $1.30 = $39,000 a year; the insert does not decompose variable cost, so this is only an upper bound, but even a smaller increase erodes the $12.00 contribution on every unit.

Conclusion: The 9.3% rise in parcel and packaging costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every one of the 30,000 units, directly threatens the $26.00 price and $12.00 contribution, and cannot be neutralised by fixing a loan rate. The interest rise is small at about $3,000 a year and the wage rise depends on hours not given in the insert, so both are secondary; TNR should renegotiate courier rates and consider passing part of the increase on through its click-and-collect option.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to TNR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TNR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of TNR with a well-justified judgement that parcel cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
